translation: The perfected persons of antiquity, having penetrated the transformations of yin and yang and investigated the boundary of life and death, compiled the Suwen, which entirely says that man takes the stomach qi as his root. Because man comes to life by receiving the qi of water and grain — what is called the clear qi, the nutritive qi, the defensive qi, and the spring-ascending qi are all alternate names of the stomach qi. Now the stomach is the sea of water and grain. When food and drink enter the stomach, the essential qi roams and overflows, ascending to be transmitted to the spleen; the spleen qi disperses the essence, which ascends to return to the lung; it regulates and frees the waterways, descending to be transported to the bladder; the essence of water is distributed in four directions; the five channels proceed in parallel; united with the four seasons and the yin-yang ceasure of the five viscera, this is held to be the norm. If food and drink lose their regulation and cold and warmth are uncomfortable, then the spleen and stomach are thereby injured; and excess of joy, anger, anxiety, fear, and toil depletes the Original Qi. When the spleen and stomach are already vacuous and declining, and the Original Qi is insufficient, the heart fire alone is over-prosperous. The heart fire is the yin fire; it arises from the lower burner, and its connection ties to the heart. The heart does not preside over orders; the minister-fire acts in its place. The minister-fire, the fire of the pericardium [channel] of the lower burner, is the bandit of the Original Qi. Fire and Original Qi cannot both stand; if one conquers, the other loses. When the spleen-stomach qi is vacuous, it flows downward to the kidney and liver, and the yin fire is thereby able to seize its earth position. Hence in the patterns of the spleen and stomach, at the beginning: the qi being high, [there is] wheezing; the body hot and vexed; its pulse surging and large, with headache; or unceasing thirst; the skin not able to withstand wind and cold, and giving rise to cold and heat. Because the yin fire gushes upward, then the qi is high and [there is] wheezing; with the body hot, vexed, [there is] headache, [there is] thirst, and the pulse is surging and large. The spleen-stomach qi flowing downward causes the grain qi not to ascend and float, so the order of growth and engendering is not carried out; then there is no yang to guard its Nutritive and Defensive [qi], and not being able to withstand wind and cold, cold and heat arise. These all arise from insufficiency of the spleen-stomach qi. Nevertheless, this is quite similar to the pattern obtained from external contraction of wind-cold, but the principle is different. Internal injury of the spleen and stomach wounds its qi; external contraction of wind-cold wounds its form. Wounding the external is excess; excess should be drained. Wounding the internal is insufficiency; insufficiency should be supplemented. Sweating, draining downward, vomiting, and restraining are all draining; warming, harmonizing, regulating, and nourishing are all supplementing. In the disease of insufficiency from internal injury, if one mistakenly recognizes it as a disease of excess from external contraction and instead drains it, then one makes the vacuous more vacuous. The Nanjing states: "Making the excess more excess and the vacuous more vacuous, depleting the insufficient and augmenting the excess — those who die thus are killed by the physician." If that is so, what then? [The answer] says: One should only use sweet-warm medicinals to supplement its center and raise its yang, and sweet-cold to drain its fire; then it [is] cured. The Suwen states: "In toil, warm it; in debilitation, warm it." Because warmth can eliminate great heat. One greatly forbids bitter-cold medicinals to drain the stomach earth. Thus I establish the Buying Zhongqi Tang (Tonify-the-Center Augment-Qi Decoction).
